title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
description: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim
body: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette KressByKali HaysTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 18 November 2026Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."   Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader."The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry."It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects"."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection."With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

schema.headline: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang

title: COP31: Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is lagging behind
description: Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is burstin
body: Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel."In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%"."People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state."You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy."We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether."The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.But it's also at a crossroads."There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed."We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up."The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

schema.headline: COP31: Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is lagging behind

title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
description: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a
body: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment. "In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.Four other owners then had the painting.The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

schema.headline: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history

title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
description: US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airpor
body: US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly sneaked onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland. Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick. American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment."As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing. "This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows. "O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

schema.headline: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe

title: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
description: The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her
body: The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure. The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through". But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system. Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening. "We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said. Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover. The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated. "Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update. Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January 2017.At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species. The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

schema.headline: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo

title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
description: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Ku
body: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law"."The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran."If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

schema.headline: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island

title: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, tell
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot."We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor. Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people."Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages."There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC."There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."Beevers said AI is only part of the story."It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said."Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

schema.headline: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US

title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
description: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message
body: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch."TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

schema.headline: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US

title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for more than $1.4tn stock market debut
description: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.The artificial intelligence (A
body: Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable. The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins. There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years. "Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary."Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind. It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so. Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money."AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".With additional reporting by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia

schema.headline: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for more than $1.4tn stock market debut

title: Putin's Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says
description: Figure caption, Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attackByClaire KeenanThe Crimean Bridge has been attacked by
body: Figure caption, Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attackByClaire KeenanThe Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 NovemberIt comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

schema.headline: Putin's Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says

title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
description: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff m
body: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff membersTwo women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment. But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February. The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations. In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions. The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

schema.headline: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences

title: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
description: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private resi
body: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

schema.headline: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour

title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
description: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kreml
body: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin. Whatever the outcome.Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed."We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."But what of those who are not at the table?Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe."We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

schema.headline: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin

title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
description: Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for resi
body: Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops"."IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter.""We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line

title: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
description: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Par
body: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase. While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high."What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added. He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs."This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted. But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle. Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties."We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF."The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation."When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air"."There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges."The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

schema.headline: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
